Introduction to the scientific study of human social interaction with particular focus on the mutual influences between individuals and the groups to which they belong; the basic theories, concepts and techniques used by sociologists in their research.

Instructor 
Bhandari, Kaufman

Sociologists and other social scientists must describe and interpret social facts in order to make sense of the world around them. To do this, they often rely on the analysis of quantitative data using statistical methods. This course acts as a primer to sociological statistical analysis. Students will learn to find and access social data, summarize patterns in that data, represent these patterns graphically, and explore relationships between different variables. Topics include descriptive measures, hypothesis testing, analysis of variance, chi-square, correlation, and regression. This course is designed as a gateway to quantitative sociological research, and emphasis is on practice and implementation, with students also learning to use SPSS software.


Satisfies the Mathematical and Quantitative Thought requirement.
 


Prerequisites

Power and Politics introduces students to political sociology, and to the study of the production, conservation and distribution of power. We are members of a democratic society: the political system is a reflection of the social system and our collective construction of both legitimate authority and the just exercise of power. For these reasons, the study of power and politics is important both as a way of gaining useful knowledge and as a vehicle for deepening one's understanding of political sociological theory.

This course explores urban transformations of the megacities in the global South. A study of global cities and their relations to emerging urbanism grows out of a simple question: "What is the source of changes to this city?" Colonialism, developmentalism, and neoliberalism remain important analytical lenses for understanding urban transformation in the global South. Through a close examination of urban transformations on these analytic perspectives, this course delves into the following topics in the global cities in Asia, Africa, and Latin America: uneven development and displacement, speculation and gentrification, governance and activism, informalization and racialization, and urban pop culture and lifestyle.

Satisfies Sociology major requirement.
Satisfies the Social-Scientific Thought requirement.
Satisfies Cultural Diversity requirement.

A brief early history, methods, theory, and concepts of social science research on health and health care mainly from the last half of the previous century to the present. We will explore gender, race, class, age, and social differences in the experiences of individuals as they deal with health and illness across their life course. The course will provide students with a sociological analysis of a broad array of health/illness issues and the health services industry.

Satisfies Public Health major and minor requirement.

Bhandari

This course examines how digital media shape culture, power, labor, and social change. Rather than treating the internet, social media, and artificial intelligence as neutral technologies, we will analyze them as social institutions embedded in capitalism and structured by race, class, gender, and global inequality. Drawing on foundational sociological thinkers such as C. Wright Mills, Max Weber, and Karl Marx, students will explore topics including influencers and digital cultural production, the manosphere and tradwife culture, algorithmic discrimination, surveillance capitalism, digital labor, artificial intelligence, and the commodification of attention. The course concludes by considering how people resist these systems and create alternative digital futures through imagination, solidarity, pleasure, and collective action. Throughout the seminar, students will connect sociological theory to contemporary digital life and ask not only how technologies transform society, but also whose interests they serve and how they might be organized differently.

Satisfies Sociology major requirement
Satisfies Social-Scientific Thought requirement
Satisfies the Justice, Equality, and Community requirement

This course is designed to provide broad overview of contemporary social theory and introduces you to the concepts, writings, and arguments of some of the most important social theorists of the 20th century. We will discuss complex interrelated cultural, social, political and economic issues and discover how social theorists have dealt with them during the decades in the 20th century when their theories were advanced. Most important, we will endeavor to understand how these issues affect our understanding of the world and the everyday lived experience. The terms and concepts we will get familiarized with are concepts such as social mechanisms, social action, social structure, as well as modernity, post-structuralism, critical theory, rational choice theory, postmodernism, and cultural studies.

This course is an introduction to the study of human language with an emphasis on Spanish. The main goal of the course is to get students familiar with the various ways in which Spanish "works" and to expose them to the basic characteristics of the language. The course introduces the Spanish sound system (phonetics and phonology), word formation (morphology), sentence structure (syntax), and meaning (semantics and pragmatics). The course discusses, as well, some of the reasons why these systems may change among Spanish speakers (variation). This class will be taught in Spanish.

This course examines literary and cultural expressions of memory and forgetting involving the Spanish Civil War. We study the periods leading up to and following the Spanish Civil War (1936-39) as well as present-day representations and recollections. Fiction and non-fictional works inform our conversations about Socialist, Communist and Fascist perspectives, as well as those from everyday men, women, and children. We pay special attention to marginalized grouops of people including Spanish women and African Americans fighting in the Spanish Civil war. Conducted in Spanish.

In this course, we will examine the relationship between politics, aesthetics, and marginality in 20th/21st-century Latin America and its Latinx diasporas in the United States. Examining marginality in various Latin American and Latinx contexts-queer and trans stigma in Mexico and Argentina; racial and economic precarity in Special Period Cuba; and intersections of race, class, and language in Nuyorican and Chicanx diasporas-we will explore the role of stigmatizing forms of representation in enacting political exclusions. Subsequently, we will explore how Latin American and Latinx authors, artists, musicians, and filmmakers find beauty in stigmatized spaces and bodies, and how this beauty offers the promise of better worlds that we might create.

Research and writing of the honors thesis begins in SPA 498 (in the spring of the junior year or the fall of the senior year) and is completed in SPA 499 during the last semester of the senior year. SPA 498 requires a thesis outline, annotated bibliography, progress reports, and an introductory chapter. An oral defense of the honors thesis proposal is held at the end of SPA 498. What do Lady Gaga, Jeff Bezos, and Leonardo DaVinci have in common? Creative thinking. While creativity might seem a little like the mythical unicorn, with fundamental training, it is possible to discover and hone a creative mindset. This class introduces students to the skills and strategies associated with the creative process as a means to increase productivity and bring deeper and richer meaning to life, both professionally and personally.  Students will explore the definition of creativity and examine it as a fundamental component for success and innovation in many fields. By researching various theoretical approaches to the creative process, students will explore how to build their own creative workflow that allows the generation of exciting ideas and the incorporation of flexibility and problem solving skills to bring those ideas to fruition.

In this course students will research their chosen honors thesis subject, and design plans to complete their scholarly and/or creative year-long project. Students will learn about multiple research methodologies deployed in the fields of theatre studies and theatrical performance, along with processes for giving and receiving feedback on work-in-progress. In this course students will: research the scholarly and artistic context for their chosen thesis subject, design a step-by-step process for completion of the project, learn established methods for critically engaging feedback on artistic work, revise written work and plans for creative work based on feedback received, and formally reflect on each step of the process. Given the individualized nature of such a course, students will toggle between independent work, one-on-one feedback sessions with the instructor, and group meetings with peers.

Satisfies Theatre major requirement.

Instructor
Riemer, Botero

XPL 199 enables students to engage in personal, professional, cultural and academically relevant experiences for academic credit.  Students engage immersive, reflective learning experiences with guidance and support from High Impact Practices (HIP) centers.  Students in each section of XPL 199 participate in similar types of HIP experiences, individualized and tailored to their needs and interests. Students gather once every other week with the instructors, to reflect on their experiences with other members of the Davidson community, share critical learning moments, and seek peer guidance. A minimum of one section of the course is offered each semester. 

Students should contact the instructor, as there is an application process for this course. Note: The B section in the fall of 2026 is reserved for pre-health students. See the application for more information.
